did_you_know.text: In the Bible, the “heart” is not only the seat of emotion but also of thought, will, and decision. Thus, “hardening the heart” describes stubborn refusal.
The verse emphasizes that historical memory is passed from one generation to the next, even to a grandchild. The story of the past helps shape identity in the present.
The Hebrew word arbeh can describe a swarm of locusts, not just a single insect. Locust swarms can migrate and quickly destroy large areas of vegetation.
The phrase “Egypt is lost” is a vivid way of saying that Egypt is ruined or in great danger; it does not mean that the country literally disappeared.
The question “Who exactly is going?” sounds like an attempt to decide who will be allowed to leave. Pharaoh still treats the departure as a limited concession, not full freedom.
The east wind blows from the east; in Egypt, dry and hot winds could carry dust and quickly change the environment. Here, the wind also brings the locust swarm.
The name Yam Suf is probably connected with the Hebrew word suf, which can refer to reeds or water plants. The exact location of this body of water is still debated.
The expression “a darkness that could be felt” is rare and difficult to translate. Different translations describe it as tangible, thick, or almost touchable darkness.
The contrast between darkness in Egypt and light in the Israelites’ settlements presents the plague not only as a natural disaster, but also as a distinction between the two groups.

“Not a single hoof will remain” is an expression of completeness: all the livestock will leave, with nothing left behind. Moses also explains that they do not yet know what will be needed for worship.
